explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The LORD says, "Come out of her, My people!" (Jeremiah 51:45). Two things stand out to me here: He calls them "My people," and the word is to leave. When He calls His own, the move is to go.

I get the thought, because loyalty is a good instinct. But the verse never sends anyone to the walls. The LORD says, "Come out of her, My people!" That's like hearing the timer go off and grabbing a spatula to guard the oven. Nope, you step away.
Making peace sounds so polite, doesn't it? But there's no treaty talk in this verse. The LORD says, "Come out of her, My people!" (Jeremiah 51:45). The call is to leave, not to negotiate.
Lives is the word. The LORD says, "Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD." Notice the "each of you." Every single person is counted, and nobody gets left in the pile.

Homes would be a natural guess, since leaving one is hard. But the verse doesn't mention homes at all. It says, "Save your lives, each of you…" (Jeremiah 51:45). The LORD cares about the people first.
Gold would be tempting to grab on the way out the door, friend. But this verse is only about the people. The LORD says, "Save your lives, each of you…" (Jeremiah 51:45). It names lives, not luggage.

True. The LORD says, "Do not let your heart grow faint, and do not be afraid when the rumor is heard in the land." Those rumors are about violence and ruler against ruler (Jeremiah 51:46). Scary news was coming, and I think He wanted their hearts steady before it arrived.

The text says the opposite, baker. The LORD tells them, "Do not let your heart grow faint, and do not be afraid when the rumor is heard in the land…" (Jeremiah 51:46). The rumors would come one year and then another the next year. So the word to His people is to stay steady, not to panic.

It's a natural guess, because you'd expect the whole world to sigh over a fallen empire. But the verse says something else. "Then heaven and earth and all that is in them will shout for joy over Babylon because the destroyers from the north will come against her" (Jeremiah 51:48). Shouting for joy is not mourning, friend.

False is right. The verse says heaven and earth "will shout for joy over Babylon," and it gives the reason: "because the destroyers from the north will come against her" (Jeremiah 51:48). This is a heavy passage, but notice that the whole creation is pictured on one side here. The mourning isn't what the verse describes.

Yes, and this is a heavy line. The verse says Babylon must fall "on account of the slain of Israel, just as the slain of all the earth have fallen because of Babylon" (Jeremiah 51:49). It puts the two groups side by side. Babylon's fall is tied to the ones who fell because of her.

explanations.answer: They will be avenged by Israel
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable thought, but the verse doesn't hand the job to Israel. It says Babylon must fall "just as the slain of all the earth have fallen because of Babylon" (Jeremiah 51:49). The text only says the slain of all the earth fell because of her.

That sounds warm and lovely, friend, but it isn't in this verse. What it says is that "the slain of all the earth have fallen because of Babylon" (Jeremiah 51:49). It's a heavy line, and it simply names who they fell because of.

That's it, baker. The verse says, "Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind" (Jeremiah 51:50). Notice the order, with the LORD first. Even from far away, their minds are told where to turn.

I can see why you'd pick it, since people love a good souvenir. But the verse points their thoughts somewhere else. It says, "Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind" (Jeremiah 51:50). Nobody's asked to remember the treasure.

That one tugs at the heart, friend. But this verse doesn't mention people left behind. It says, "Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind" (Jeremiah 51:50). The LORD and Jerusalem are the two things named.

explanations.answer: Foreigners entered the LORD's holy places
explanations.explanation: Yes. The speakers say, "disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD's house" (Jeremiah 51:51). I think this one hurts, and the verse says it plainly. The reason is right there in the text.

explanations.answer: Their own king abandoned the city
explanations.explanation: That would be a rough thing to live through. But the verse doesn't mention a king leaving. It says, "disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD's house" (Jeremiah 51:51).

explanations.answer: Their harvest failed two years running
explanations.explanation: Two bad years in a row would sting, friend. But a harvest never comes up in these verses. The reason given is "because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD's house" (Jeremiah 51:51). The shame is about the LORD's house.

True. The LORD says, "Even if Babylon ascends to the heavens and fortifies her lofty stronghold, the destroyers I send will come against her" (Jeremiah 51:53). Picture hiding on the very top shelf so nobody finds you. A high spot doesn't matter if the One who sends them already knows where you are.

The text says it will happen anyway. "Even if Babylon ascends to the heavens and fortifies her lofty stronghold, the destroyers I send will come against her" (Jeremiah 51:53). I'd have bet on that tall stronghold too, friend. But the LORD says height doesn't change the outcome.
Right. The verse says, "For the LORD will destroy Babylon; He will silence her mighty voice" (Jeremiah 51:55). Her big, loud voice goes quiet. That's a strong word for a city that had a lot to say.
You'd think a mighty voice would carry farther and farther. But the verse says the opposite. "He will silence her mighty voice" (Jeremiah 51:55). The volume goes down, not out.
Ha, a little solo for Babylon. But no song is on the program, friend. The LORD says, "He will silence her mighty voice" (Jeremiah 51:55). Silence is the word.
That's the one. The verse says, "the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full" (Jeremiah 51:56). Notice "in full." Nothing is left half done.

Rebuilding isn't what this verse says. It says, "the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full" (Jeremiah 51:56). And two verses later her thick walls will be leveled (Jeremiah 51:58). Picking up the blocks again isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: He will give her more time
explanations.explanation: More time would be a kind thing to hope for, friend. But the verse says something different. "He will repay in full" (Jeremiah 51:56). The text doesn't hand her an extension.

It sounds like a long nap, doesn't it? But the verse says this sleep is different. "Then they will fall asleep forever and not wake up" (Jeremiah 51:57). That's a heavy line, and it doesn't leave a morning after.

False is right. The LORD says, "Then they will fall asleep forever and not wake up," declares the King (Jeremiah 51:57). It's a heavy word, so I'll say it plainly. There's no waking up the next morning.
Yes, baker. The verse says, "declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts" (Jeremiah 51:57). The word about Babylon's leaders comes from the King Himself. He gives His own name right there.
That's a real title in Scripture, friend. It shows up in Daniel 7:9. But it isn't the name this verse gives. Here the King's name is "the LORD of Hosts" (Jeremiah 51:57).

You're not making that one up, since the title appears in Isaiah 49:26. It just isn't the one in this verse. Jeremiah 51:57 says, "declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts." The text names the King right there.
Yes. The LORD of Hosts says, "Babylon's thick walls will be leveled, and her high gates consumed by fire" (Jeremiah 51:58). The walls fall and the gates burn. Both go together.
Open gates would be a friendly picture, but that isn't this verse. It says her "high gates consumed by fire" (Jeremiah 51:58). Nobody's rolling out a welcome mat.
A fresh bronze coat sounds fancy, friend. But the verse has no polish for these gates. It says, "her high gates consumed by fire" (Jeremiah 51:58).

I'd love to say yes, since years of building should count for something. But the LORD of Hosts says otherwise. "So the labor of the people will be for nothing" (Jeremiah 51:58). Nothing means nothing, friend.

False is right. The LORD of Hosts says, "So the labor of the people will be for nothing; the nations will exhaust themselves to fuel the flames" (Jeremiah 51:58). All that effort doesn't last. It just feeds the fire.
